turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she turned to Jack, her voice dripping with disdain. She told him that his family, connections, and social standing were of the utmost importance, and that she would not be satisfied with anything less than a satisfactory explanation of his background.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he did not have a family, and that he was raised by his strict and elderly aunt

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned skeptical as she asked, 'And I suppose this aunt of yours, Mr. Worthing, was a woman of great refinement and breeding?'

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted that her mother should not be questioning Mr. Worthing's character and background, and that she knew him well enough to trust him.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen to refrain from intervening in this matter, as her mother's concerns about Mr. Worthing's suitability as a husband for her daughter took precedence over any feelings of loyalty or affection.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had always been aware of the importance of social standing and had made an effort to educate himself, but his aunt had not encouraged him to think about his family's connections.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern as she told Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing that she had every right to be concerned about the potential union, given the uncertainty surrounding Mr. Worthing's family connections and background.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen stood up straight and insisted that she would not be ignored in this conversation, that her feelings and opinions mattered.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that she would not be swayed by his protestations of familiarity with her daughter, and that she would press on with her inquiries to determine his suitability as a husband.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Mr. Worthing asked if Lady Bracknell's concerns about his family's connections were not, in fact, already being addressed through his marriage to her daughter, Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that his attempt to deflect her concerns was quite unconvincing, and that she would not be satisfied with vague assurances about his suitability as a husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he understood Lady Bracknell's concerns and was willing to provide any information she needed about his family's connections.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing to provide proof of his family's respectable connections, and to reveal the circumstances of his birth, as she suspected that there may be more to his story than he had initially let on.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that his father was a large and impressive man, and that he had passed away when Jack was still very young, as he had been in the habit of doing for many years.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing to explain the circumstances of his father's death, and to provide a detailed account of his family's business dealings.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack replied that his father's death had been due to a long illness, and that his mother had managed the family business after his passing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen asked to be let out of the carriage, her voice rising in annoyance at the prolonged questioning.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that Mr. Worthing provide a full and satisfactory explanation of his father's illness and business dealings, and warned him that she would not be satisfied with vague or evasive answers.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not be kept waiting any longer, and that she expected a decision about the marriage to be made soon.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that it would be unbecoming for a young lady of her standing to become impatient in the face of a few, albeit necessary, inquiries about the gentleman she proposes to marry.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
